community-s6h/u1-emuA:
Access to medical care is often one of the trickiest connections to make. While some communities may want to focus on “natural” medical care, someone in the community may end up needing trauma surgery, antibiotics, dental care, obstetric emergency care, or any number of other specialized medical services. As a community, it’s important to discuss and decide how community members should be able to access medical care. What kind of care will the community guarantee to its members out of common money? What kinds of care may require members to use outside sources of money or insurance? What will the community do if some members choose to receive (or not receive) different kinds of medical care?

It’s important that community members not be forced to jump through ideological hoops when they are scared and/or sick. If a community member becomes catastrophically ill, it’s important that pre-existing agreements are in place so that the sick community member’s choices are protected, they can access community resources and/or outside sources of money, they can be transported to get care if they choose, and their privacy is maintained, among other things. It may be that the “natural” or otherwise preferred method of medical care is not enough.

Social connections are an important part of being healthy. According to a Surgeon General’s Advisory, socially isolated people are at increased risk for a variety of health outcomes. While community is not a panacea, it can make a huge difference in the conditions under which community members become ill, heal from illnesses, age, and eventually die.
community-s6h/u1-emuB:
Connection around medical care is a really tough one. Communities will want to be sure to talk about how medical care will be accessed. If the community wants to be all natural, what will they do when someone wants/needs trauma surgery, antibiotics, dentistry, obstetric emergency care, etc, etc, etc? It is important for a community to talk through how they will make sure that each member has access to the medical care that she/he needs/wants. It may be a good idea to talk through what kind of care the community will guarantee access to using community common resources, and what kind of care will need to be accessed by other means, such as outside dollars or insurance. It is also important to talk about how the community will deal with people choosing to accept or not to accept varying levels of medical care.

It should not be necessary for a community member to have to jump through hoops, especially ideological ones, when they are scared and/or sick. It is good to have agreements in place ahead of time so that in the case of catastrophic illness for a community member, that person's choices are protected, they can have access to common resources and/or outside funds, they can be transported to receive care if they choose, and their privacy is maintained, and that the community is prepared for the possibility that the "community way" of dealing with medical care may not be enough.

Related to this, social connection is very important for good health. The Surgeon General's advisory states that socially isolated individuals are at increased risk for a variety of health outcomes. While community is not a panacea, it can make a big difference in the conditions in which a person becomes sick, heals from sickness, ages, and even dies.

This can be one of the trickiest connections to deal with. A community may prefer to provide or support natural medical care for its members, but what if someone needs trauma surgery, antibiotics, dental work, obstetric care, etc? It's important for the community to hash out how community members will gain access to the medical care they need. What will be covered by the community using community resources? What will require outside dollars or insurance? What if someone wants (or doesn't want) a certain level of care?

It's important that no one has to jump through ideological hoops when they're scared and sick. It's also important that if a community member becomes catastrophically ill, there are agreements already in place to make sure their choices are respected, that they have access to common resources or outside funds as needed, that they are able to get where they need to go, that their privacy is maintained, and that the community has considered the possibility that the methods they prefer might not be enough.

One thing to keep in mind is that being connected to others is good for a person's health. The Surgeon General's advisory on social isolation notes increased risk for a variety of health outcomes for isolated people. Community isn't a panacea, but it can make a difference in the conditions under which people get sick, heal, age, and die.
